segments.text: Shine white light on a surface with fine, regular grooves, like a CD, and it fans out into rainbows.
Stack thin, clear layers, like those in a morpho butterfly's wing, and they reflect one vivid colour.
No pigment anywhere. So how can mere structure pick a direction, and a colour?
It all comes down to one idea: symmetry.
Start with the simplest structure: a flat boundary, with glass below and air above.
Remember from episode one: a plane wave's tilt is set by kx, its frequency along x. Then sin θ = kx/k.
In glass the wavelength shrinks, so k grows to n·k0, where n is the refractive index. Each medium gets its own circle.
The field can't jump at the boundary, so the crests on both sides must meet. Both waves share one kx: it's conserved, like momentum.
In k-space, a shared kx is one vertical line. Where it crosses each circle, you read off each wave's direction. That's Snell's law, in one picture.
Now tilt the incoming wave further. The line slides outward, and soon it misses the air circle completely.
No wave in air has that kx, so all the light reflects, leaving only an evanescent tail. That's total internal reflection.
Now give the boundary a pattern that repeats every Λ, the period. That's a grating.
Anything that repeats like this is a Fourier series: a sum of waves e^(imKx), where K = 2π/Λ.
Passing through the grating multiplies the light by these waves, and each one shifts kx by mK.
So kx is now conserved only up to multiples of K. In k-space: copies of the line, spaced by K.
Each copy that crosses the circle is a beam that can leave: a diffraction order.
Colour sets the circle. Red light has a smaller circle than blue, so the same K bends red the most: a rainbow.
Now shrink the period. K grows, and the orders leave the circle, one by one.

At normal incidence into air, a period below the air wavelength leaves only the transmitted zero order. Internal resonances can remain, so treating the grating as a uniform film needs a separate check.
Now let the structure repeat along the direction light travels: a stack of layers, repeating every period.
Shift it by one period and nothing changes. So the waves inside can only gain a fixed phase from one period to the next.
These are Bloch waves: e^(iκz) times a function that repeats. A full turn of phase per period is invisible, so κ only matters up to multiples of K.
Plot frequency, ω, against κ. With no contrast, light follows a straight line, and its copies, shifted by K, are the same waves.
The copies cross at the zone edge, where λ = 2nΛ. That's the Bragg condition: reflections from every layer add up in step.
Now turn up the index contrast, Δn. Watch the crossing: the forward and backward waves couple, and the bands pull apart.
A gap opens: a band of frequencies where no wave can travel through the stack.
Light there dies off within a few layers, so it all reflects. Ten pairs make a nearly perfect mirror for one band of colours.
How do you compute a real grating, with thick ridges? Rigorous coupled-wave analysis, RCWA, puts all of this together.
Thanks to the period, the field in any layer is just a list of amplitudes, one per diffraction order.
In a uniform layer, each order travels alone, picking up its own phase, e^(ikz z). The matrix is diagonal, as in episode one.
In a grating layer, the Fourier coefficients of ε couple each order to the others, and the matrix fills in.
Diagonalize it: the eigenvectors are the layer's Bloch modes, and the eigenvalues give their kz.
Advance each mode's phase, match the fields at every interface, and chain the layers with scattering matrices. They never contain growing exponentials, so they stay stable.
On a computer, RCWA takes four lines: expand ε, build the matrix, diagonalize, chain the layers.
The pitfall is truncation: keep enough orders, and check that the answer converges. For the other polarization, use Li's factorization rules.
The payoff: sweep the ridge width of a sub-wavelength grating, and record the phase of the light passing straight through.
That's a metasurface's unit-cell library. Pick the width for each phase you need, and you have a flat lens, cell by cell.
Symmetry fixes momentum. Flat interfaces conserve kx. Periodic ones conserve it only up to multiples of K = 2π/Λ, and where copies meet, gaps open.
Where it breaks: RCWA needs true periodicity, and a metasurface lens only borrows it locally, cell by cell.
Total internal reflection traps light in a slab, and Bragg mirrors trap it between them. So how do we guide light, and store it?
